prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength are interrogated simultaneously, bringing frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B012 as the only prize part, with Katori and Ye. After reading the full first-round exchange, the scientific case rests on one distinct idea. At the magic wavelength the light shifts of the two clock states cancel, so the trap perturbs the transition only negligibly while thousands of atoms are held free of Doppler and recoil shifts. Many atoms measured at once give a statistical gain that a single trapped ion cannot provide, and that is what moved stability and accuracy together toward 10^-18. The result is reproduced in several species and by independent laboratories on several continents, and it is already used for relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and the preparation of a redefinition of the second. Seven of eight round-1 files reach this configuration for consistent reasons, but I am relying on the reasons and not the count. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: a concept originator and a leader who brought the instrument to record performance. I have tightened my citation so that it names many-atom interrogation at the magic wavelength, which is the step the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-ion prize did not honour.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses remain. First, lattice-clock credit is wider than two names: Takamoto and colleagues, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke, and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups all contributed, and I cannot settle the strontium versus ytterbium first-demonstration history from the files. A citation can describe the concept and its realisation, but it cannot make the omissions disappear, and Danielsson is right that this could still be judged unfair. Second, comparable uncertainty has been reached with single-ion clocks, so the case must not rest on accuracy alone. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened. I do not treat it as a precondition, but Eriksson's view that the full impact is unfinished is a respectable position. Finally, I am a theoretical atomic physicist and may overvalue the atomic-structure elegance relative to conceptual advances in condensed matter.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps B030 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as his sole preference because a concept that changed how a class of materials is understood should outrank a precision-measurement advance, and he treats the pending redefinition of the second as leaving the clock's impact unfinished.
responses.response: I accept the force of the conceptual argument, and I ranked B030 second because I think the Z2 invariant and the HgTe observation are first-rate. I do not think the lattice clock is merely an instrument, because the magic-wavelength condition is itself a piece of atomic-structure insight about state-independent trapping, and it is what makes the measurement possible. On the redefinition, the 10^-18 performance has been reproduced and compared across laboratories, so the achievement exists independently of any metrological timetable. On B030 I would put the question the other way: even if a citation naming the HgTe observation is fair to Molenkamp, it omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose prediction that experiment tested, and the three-dimensional work. With the three-person cap I do not see a fair repair, which is why B030 stays an alternative for me. I would be glad to hear whether the citation wording I now propose, anchored on the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation, meets your novelty concern.

responses.point: Johansson cautions that ion clocks reach comparable uncertainty and that part of the precision-measurement story was credited in 2012, so the citation should be anchored on the magic-wavelength lattice and not on accuracy in general.
responses.response: I accept the correction and I have changed my citation accordingly. My round-1 wording, in particular the phrase about building on but not duplicating earlier prizes, was too loose, because single-ion clocks do reach comparable uncertainty. What distinguishes the lattice clock is the interrogation of a large ensemble of neutral atoms in a state-independent trap. That route to high stability is not available for a single ion, and it does not depend on the 2012 methods of controlling one quantum system. The citation therefore names the magic-wavelength lattice and the simultaneous interrogation of many atoms, and it does not name accuracy as the achievement. I also share your doubt about the Sr and Yb first-demonstration history.

responses.point: Danielsson asked me to say explicitly how the citation should separate neutral-atom lattice interrogation from the single-ion clocks that earlier work built on, and asks whether the overlap with 2005 and 2012 has been checked, noting that others also ask whether the omission of other lattice-clock pioneers makes a two-name prize unfair.
responses.response: The citation should contain three elements that single-ion clocks do not have: neutral atoms, a lattice at the magic wavelength so that the clock transition is unperturbed by the trap, and simultaneous interrogation of many atoms. That is how I have worded it. On the overlap check, from the atomic physics I can say that the lattice clock rests on a different mechanism from the comb, which measures and counts optical frequencies, and from Wineland's single-ion control, which isolates one quantum system. On fairness, I think the omissions are better handled by wording than by adding names. Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke and the national laboratories are real contributors, but the statutes ask for a discovery or invention and its credited originators, and Katori for the concept and Ye for taking the instrument to record performance is a defensible account. I cannot confirm the first-demonstration details from here, so I flag this as the main open risk.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the redefinition of the second should not be a precondition, and says the two-way risk of overlap with earlier prizes is symmetric because the 2012 prizes did not block the 2025 circuit award. He would also not put B030 in a preferred configuration because of the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang gap.
responses.response: I agree on both points and the second one is where we most closely coincide. The comparison with 2012 and 2025 is useful but, to be careful, it shows only that earlier prizes in a broad area do not block a later one. It is not a substitute for showing that the new idea is distinct, which is why I rely on the magic-wavelength argument and not on precedent. I part from you only slightly on B030. I think the HgTe observation is a strong experimental half and Eriksson is right that the concept is mature. The decisive point for me is that the attribution gap cannot be repaired within the cap, so I keep B030 as an alternative but not as a preferred part.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, now ranks B012 first while conceding that B042 has the larger recent scientific footprint, and says the attribution for B042 is less settled than he assumed.
responses.response: I agree with the concession on attribution, and I think it matters more than the size of the literature. My position on B042 is unchanged in substance: Bistritzer and MacDonald's continuum model and the 2018 experiments opened a major field, but the origin of the superconductivity and of other correlated states is unsettled, and the experimental credit is divided among groups that three names cannot cover. I regard B042 as a serious candidate for a later year. It stays an alternative for me, and I would be willing to see it as lead if the mechanism and the credit question become clearer, which I expect to take a year or two.

uncertainties: The first-demonstration attribution among strontium and ytterbium lattice clocks, and the weight due to Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, cannot be settled from the materials provided to me. This is the main risk to a two-name prize.
Whether a prize rested on measured performance should wait for the redefinition of the second. I judge it need not, but Eriksson holds a reasonable contrary view.
Whether the committee will treat an instrument achievement as equal in standing to a conceptual discovery such as topological insulators; Eriksson and Mehlig both name this as open.
Whether a second prize part is warranted. With a three-person cap, any second part would carry a single name from B030 or B042, which I do not consider a fair allocation.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the preferred B012 configuration (Katori, Ye). For disclosure only: my profile documents a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, papers with the Lund attosecond group, and collaboration with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich. None of these is a credited name on B012, B030 or B042. Wallraff of B005 is at ETH Zurich, but no relationship with him is documented and B005 is not part of my position. I make no other connection claim.
